system.name: Autothrottle
system.one_liner: a practical bi-level resource management system for SLO-targeted microservices

components.name: Tower
components.role: application-level learning-based controller that observes end-to-end latency/workload and sets performance targets

components.name: Captain
components.role: per-service heuristic controller that meets the performance target set by the Tower

components.name: CPU scheduler
components.role: enforces the throttle/quota decided by its Captain and reports CPU usage back

components.name: Application
components.role: the microservice application graph the Tower and Captains manage

components.name: Gateway
components.role: entry point into the microservice application graph

content.key_idea: Autothrottle decouples application-wide SLO feedback from per-service resource control: a single learning-based Tower observes end-to-end latency and workload to periodically set CPU throttle-ratio performance targets, and per-service Captains locally translate those targets into CPU scheduler quotas.
content.reading_order: the microservice Application graph at the bottom feeds RPS/latency up to the Tower at top-left, which sets performance targets for a zoomed-in Captain at top-right, which in turn manages its local CPU scheduler.

summary: Autothrottle manages CPU resources for SLO-targeted microservices with a bi-level design. Figure 2 shows a green 'Tower (§3.3)' box at top-left receiving RPS and latency signals from the microservice 'Application' graph below it, which is entered through a 'Gateway' icon and drawn as a small DAG of blue server nodes. The Tower fans dotted lines out to per-service controllers and periodically sends each a performance target, expressed as a CPU throttle ratio; one of these, labeled 'Captain (§3.2)', is shown zoomed in on the right, receiving the CPU-allocation/performance-target exchange with the Tower and, inside its own box, managing a 'CPU scheduler' via throttle, usage and quota signals. This layout captures the paper's core idea of decoupling application-level SLO feedback (handled once by the Tower) from service-level resource control (handled independently and locally by each Captain).
